turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in. Sorry the waiting room was so full this morning.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Please do not apologise. I am grateful you could see me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course. What brings you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I have a cough which has lasted six weeks. It came on after a bout of flu, and it has not cleared.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks is a fair stretch. Tell me about that flu, would you.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I was in bed for about ten days with a fever. That was, well, about eight weeks ago. The fever settled, but the cough did not.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the cough dry, or do you bring up phlegm?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It is mostly dry, Doctor. In the mornings there is a small amount of clear phlegm. It is never coloured.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood at all?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not coughed up any blood.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): When is it at its worst?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It is much worse at night. I wake with it. It is present in the daytime as well, only less so.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your breathing?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I am a little short of breath on the stairs. On the flat I am perfectly all right. I do not wheeze.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever now, or sweats in the night?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever since the flu, and no night sweats. I feel quite myself in that regard.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I have not lost weight.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any travel abroad recently, or contact with anyone who has tuberculosis?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No recent travel. And no, I have not been in contact with tuberculosis.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I take one small glass of wine with dinner on a Saturday, and that is all.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you working at the moment?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I am retired. I left the Department five years ago.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. Medicines, then. What do you take regularly?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, ten milligrams, by mouth, one tablet every morning, for my blood pressure. I have been on it for years.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else in the last while, even a short course?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): During the flu the out-of-hours doctor prescribed amoxicillin. He first said two hundred and fifty milligrams, then he corrected himself to five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for five days. I finished every dose. I am not taking it now.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough mixture or inhaler?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No inhaler. At night I take one spoonful, by mouth, of a brown cough bottle from the chemist. I am sorry, I cannot recall the name of it. It scarcely helps.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's fine. We won't guess the name. Does anyone at home take medicines that could be confused with yours?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife takes metformin for her diabetes. I believe it is five hundred milligrams, but it is hers alone, and I have never taken it. My sister often urges me to try biotin, as she does, and I have not taken that either.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to any drug?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): None. I have never had an allergic reaction.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any history of asthma, or anything else ongoing besides the blood pressure?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No asthma. The blood pressure is the only thing that continues. I should mention that about two years ago the hospital did a chest x-ray, and they said it was borderline, something to do with the size of the heart. Nobody followed it up with me.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so we'll note that old film as borderline on heart size, without treating it as a firm result. The blood pressure is the condition we already know about.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. That is correct.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stomach, waterworks, the rest of you, any trouble there?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Those systems are entirely in order.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Before I examine you, you look as if the morning has already been long.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Indeed. I left the house in plenty of time, and still the traffic on the N11 was at a standstill. I was twenty minutes just getting past the Bray turn.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I came the same way. The rain has the whole of the coast road crawling. Did you see the state of the sky over the Sugar Loaf?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I did. It was black as ink, and then a gap of blue for about five minutes, and then it closed over again. Very Irish, if I may say.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): My granddaughter was meant to have her school sports on the green this afternoon. I rang my daughter at breakfast and she said they have moved the whole thing into the hall.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a pity for the children. My own grandson, Ciarán, had his hurling blitz cancelled last Saturday for the very same reason. He was dressed in the kit from half seven, and then the text came.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): How old is he now?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): He is eight. Mad for the hurling, and he supports Kilkenny, though the rest of us are Dublin. We had quite a debate about it over Sunday lunch.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Kilkenny will do that to a house. Was the lunch at yours?

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): At my daughter's, in Rathmines. She made a roast, and the small fellow ate nothing but the potatoes. We stayed on for the crossword, which he is already better at than I am.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): They always are. I still buy the paper on a Saturday out of habit, and the sports pages are the only bit I finish.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I do the same. I will not pretend I understand the cricket they put on the back page in summer, but I read it all the same. It is a harmless way to spend the evening.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Harmless indeed. Right. Shall we come back to yourself?

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. Doctor, I ought to correct something I said: I told you I had not lost weight, but fastening my coat just now I saw I have taken the belt in a notch and the trousers are loose. I have lost some weight, and I could not tell you when that began.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for putting that right. We will keep it in mind, though we cannot date it. Is there anything else?

[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): One thing, if I may. I still do not believe I have had contact with tuberculosis, for I have not seen my cousin Declan since Christmas. My sister telephoned last week, though, and said he had been in hospital with a chest complaint. She thought it might be tuberculosis, but she was not sure, and it may only have been pneumonia.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I follow you. We will not call that contact, and we will not put the name tuberculosis on it either, because nobody in this room actually knows. Let me examine you.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your blood pressure today is one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-four. Your pulse is seventy-six, and it is regular.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): The temperature is thirty-six point eight degrees. Your oxygen level is ninety-seven percent, and your breathing rate is sixteen.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I think that is better than the chemist. They had me at around one hundred and fifty over ninety-five a month ago, though I did not write it down.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): We will use today's figures. The chest is clear. I do not hear crackles, and I do not hear a wheeze.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): The throat is a little red. There are no swollen glands in the neck. The heart sounds are normal, and there is no murmur.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): I am glad the chest is clear. Does the redness matter at all?

[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): A little redness can linger after a viral illness. I am thinking this through out loud with you. A cough that goes on for six weeks can have a few explanations, and I am not going to put a name on the cause today. Naming one now would only be guessing.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): I quite understand. I would sooner you were sure.
[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I will do is order a chest x-ray. It is to have a proper look, not because I have decided there is anything in particular on it.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Will that be soon, Doctor?
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will ask reception to arrange it this week. If the film shows something that needs a sample, I might send sputum then. I am not ordering the sputum today.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): And as regards medicine? I did finish the antibiotic.

[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not prescribing another antibiotic. It would not settle a cough of this sort at this stage, and I want the picture first. You may keep taking the spoonful of that cough bottle at night, though we do not know its name, and please do not start your wife's metformin or your sister's biotin.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): I should never do that. What ought I to watch for?
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you cough up blood, or the shortness of breath gets worse, or a fever returns, do not wait. Come back here, or go to the emergency department, the same day.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do so. And when should I come back to you in the ordinary course?
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we will go through the x-ray together. If the appointment for the film has not come through by Friday, ring the surgery and we will chase it.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear, and I am most grateful.

spec.situation: Cough for six weeks after flu; worse at night; patient says no weight loss, then says clothes are loose; recent travel or TB contact denied by patient but a family member recalls a cousin's illness; doctor orders chest X-ray, avoids naming a cause.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Initially denied, later uncertain cousin illness mentioned; current absence not fully secure.
Patient said around 150/95 a month ago and not written down; exact value unsupported.
bad.text: Blood pressure at the chemist (value=150/95, unit=mmHg, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Current chest x-ray was ordered, not completed.
Follow-up in two weeks is planned, but responsible person is not specifically doctor.
bad.text: Follow-up consultation (action_type=follow_up, status=planned, responsible_person=doctor, time_reference=value: in two weeks)

omissions.text: The cough is mostly dry; only a small amount of clear phlegm is produced in the mornings.
The patient wakes with the cough at night.
Shortness of breath is absent on the flat; only stairs cause mild breathlessness.
Initial denial of weight loss was corrected later by the patient: he has noticed loosening trousers/belt and has lost some weight, but cannot date when it began.

The recorded negative finding of 'tuberculosis contact absent' is overstated: the patient denied known TB contact but later reported a cousin was recently hospitalised with a chest complaint that might have been tuberculosis or might have been pneumonia, and the doctor explicitly said not to label this as TB contact.

The old chest x-ray from about two years ago was described by the patient as 'borderline' regarding heart size, and the doctor noted it as an old film borderline on heart size without treating it as a firm result.
On examination, the doctor said 'the chest is clear.'
The doctor stated he was not going to name the cause of the cough today because that would be guessing.
The planned chest x-ray is to 'have a proper look,' not because the doctor has decided there is anything in particular on it.
The doctor is not ordering a sputum sample today; it would only be sent later if the chest x-ray shows something needing a sample.
The doctor said he is not prescribing another antibiotic because it would not settle this sort of cough at this stage and he wants the picture first.
Follow-up purpose was specified: return in two weeks to go through the chest x-ray together.
